title: Antibiotics: A Practical Primer for the Inpatient Resident

slides.title: What this primer is for
paragraphs: Most antibiotic errors on the wards are not failures to remember a mechanism. They come from treating a diagnosis that is not established, choosing a drug without accounting for the site or likely resistance, missing source control, or continuing the initial regimen after better information arrives.
The focus is bedside decision-making. Use current pharmacy guidance, the local antibiogram, product labeling, and organism-specific guidelines for prescribing details.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
What this primer is for Most antibiotic errors on the wards are not failures to remember a mechanism. They come from treating a diagnosis that is not established, choosing a drug without accounting for the site or likely resistance, missing source control, or continuing the initial regimen after better information arrives. The focus is bedside decision-making. Use current pharmacy guidance, the local antibiogram, product labeling, and organism-specific guidelines for prescribing details. By the end, you should be able to Build an empiric regimen from the syndrome, severity, likely pathogens, prior microbiology, and local resistance data. Compare the practical coverage gaps of commonly used inpatient antibiotics, recognize the major restricted agents, and know when their use requires ID and pharmacy input. Recognize when dose, route, tissue penetration, toxicity, monitoring needs, or source control makes an apparently active drug a poor choice. Narrow, stop, or transition therapy when the clinical and microbiologic data permit. Explain what the major antibiotic trials did and did not establish. Use local guidance at the bedside. Check the current formulary, renal adjustment guidance, vancomycin monitoring workflow, local antibiogram, and actual susceptibility report before prescribing. This is primarily a resident primer. Residents should complete the main text. Fellows should know the same material and continue through the brief fellow section on resistance mechanisms, difficult treatment choices, and pipeline agents.

slides.title: A practical word about dosing
paragraphs: Local practice: Beta-lactam infusion practices differ across sites and may change. Do not assume standard or extended infusion from this module. Use the current site-specific order set and pharmacy guidance.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Before choosing the drug When someone asks, “What antibiotic should we use?” I usually need several other answers first. Sometimes the correct response is immediate broad therapy. Sometimes it is a better culture, drainage, or no antibiotic at all. Is there an infection? What findings support infection rather than colonization, inflammation, aspiration pneumonitis, or a contaminated specimen? How sick is the patient? Instability lowers the tolerance for missing a pathogen. A stable patient allows more diagnostic precision. Where is it? The syndrome determines likely organisms, penetration, source control, and duration. What has grown before? Review prior cultures, recent antibiotics, healthcare exposure, devices, and the local antibiogram. What will fix the source? Drainage, debridement, device removal, or relief of obstruction may matter more than adding another drug. When will we reassess? Write what you expect to know in 24–72 hours and what would allow narrowing or stopping. For students and residents Be able to state the syndrome, likely organisms, why the chosen drug covers them, what it misses, and what information will change the plan. For fellows Separate guideline recommendations from trial evidence and local practice. When several drugs are active, weigh resistance mechanism, inoculum, exposure, toxicity, source control, and the consequences of failure. A practical word about dosing Do not memorize one dose for each drug. The same antibiotic may have different doses for cystitis, bacteremia, meningitis, obesity, augmented renal clearance, intermittent hemodialysis, or continuous renal replacement therapy. Loading doses are often based on volume of distribution and may still be needed in acute kidney injury; maintenance dosing is where renal clearance usually matters. For severe infection, verify the dose before the first administration rather than waiting for the next day’s rounds. Local practice: Beta-lactam infusion practices differ across sites and may change. Do not assume standard or extended infusion from this module. Use the current site-specific order set and pharmacy guidance.

slides.title: Beta-lactams
paragraphs: Beta-lactams are the backbone of inpatient therapy. For each one, know the usual spectrum and the important gaps. The table assumes a susceptible isolate. ESBL production, AmpC risk, carbapenemases, and local resistance can completely change the answer.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Beta-lactams Beta-lactams are the backbone of inpatient therapy. For each one, know the usual spectrum and the important gaps. The table assumes a susceptible isolate. ESBL production, AmpC risk, carbapenemases, and local resistance can completely change the answer. Common inpatient beta-lactams Drug Where it is commonly useful Important gaps and cautions Ampicillin or amoxicillin Susceptible streptococci, Enterococcus faecalis , and Listeria . Klebsiella pneumoniae is intrinsically resistant to ampicillin. Activity against E. coli is too variable for routine empiric use. 12 Ampicillin-sulbactam Streptococci, MSSA, susceptible E. faecalis , oral flora, and anaerobes. Commonly used for selected head and neck, aspiration-related, skin, and polymicrobial infections. No Pseudomonas . Empiric E. coli and Klebsiella reliability depends on local susceptibility. CRAB dosing is a separate specialist use. Piperacillin-tazobactam Broad empiric coverage including susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , anaerobes, streptococci, MSSA, and many E. faecalis isolates. No MRSA. Do not assume activity against ESBL or AmpC organisms. It is not preferred definitive therapy for ESBL bloodstream infection. Cefazolin MSSA, streptococci, and susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , and Proteus mirabilis . Often preferred for MSSA infection. No enterococci, MRSA, or Pseudomonas . Not a treatment for ESBL-producing isolates. Ceftriaxone Most streptococci, most pneumococci, and many susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella . Useful for many community-onset infections. No Pseudomonas , enterococci, or MRSA. Avoid as definitive therapy for invasive infection due to organisms at moderate risk of inducible AmpC, including Enterobacter cloacae complex, Klebsiella aerogenes , Citrobacter freundii , and Hafnia alvei . 1 Cefepime Susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , MSSA, and streptococci. Relatively stable against AmpC. No anaerobes, enterococci, or MRSA. Renal adjustment is essential; unexplained encephalopathy or myoclonus should raise concern for neurotoxicity. Ertapenem ESBL-producing E. coli or Klebsiella , susceptible mixed Enterobacterales, and anaerobes when a carbapenem is indicated. No reliable Pseudomonas , Acinetobacter , enterococcal, or MRSA activity. Meropenem Serious ESBL infection, many susceptible Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas , and anaerobes. No MRSA and unreliable enterococcal activity. Preserve for situations where its spectrum or resistance stability is needed. Aztreonam Targeted aerobic gram-negative coverage, including susceptible Pseudomonas , when preferred beta-lactams cannot be used. No gram-positive or anaerobic activity and unreliable empiric coverage for many resistant gram-negative organisms. It is usually a poor empiric monotherapy choice for a seriously ill patient. Avoid routine aztreonam when a better beta-lactam can be given safely. It usually has very low cross-reactivity with other beta-lactams, but it shares an identical R1 side chain with ceftazidime. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime allergy should prompt allergy-guided review rather than routine aztreonam use. 4 21 Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole Where ceftaroline and ceftobiprole fit Drug What makes it different What residents should not assume Ceftaroline Teflaro A cephalosporin with MRSA activity. FDA-labeled uses are acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, including MRSA, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia due to designated susceptible organisms. The pneumonia indication includes MSSA, not MRSA. 22 MRSA bacteremia and endocarditis use is off-label and is supported mainly by observational salvage and combination-therapy experience, not a definitive randomized bacteremia trial. Do not count on Pseudomonas , enterococci, atypical organisms, or clinically adequate anaerobic coverage. Ceftobiprole Zevtera A cephalosporin with activity against MSSA and MRSA. FDA-labeled uses include adult S. aureus bacteremia, including right-sided endocarditis, adult acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia in adults and children at least 3 months old. 23 The bacteremia indication should not be stretched to left-sided endocarditis. It is not a dependable choice for Pseudomonas , ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, anaerobes, or atypical pneumonia pathogens. Confirm formulary status and susceptibility before use. ERADICATE provides randomized trial data for ceftobiprole in complicated S. aureus bacteremia. Ceftobiprole was noninferior to daptomycin for overall treatment success: 69.8% compared with 68.7%. The adjusted difference was 2.0 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from −7.1 to 11.1. Ceftaroline does not have comparable randomized trial evidence for MRSA bacteremia. ERADICATE also should not be extrapolated to every endovascular infection. 24 Consider Klebsiella coverage separately from E. coli . Susceptible isolates may be covered by cefazolin, ceftriaxone, cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a carbapenem, depending on the syndrome and susceptibility result. Ampicillin is not active against K. pneumoniae . A carbapenem is generally preferred for invasive ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae infection. 1 12 Resident essential: ESBL and AmpC are not interchangeable labels ESBL enzymes are most often encountered in E. coli , K. pneumoniae , and K. oxytoca and inactivate most penicillins, cephalosporins, and aztreonam. Carbapenems generally remain active. For organisms at moderate risk of clinically significant inducible AmpC, the 2026 IDSA guidance identifies E. cloacae complex, K. aerogenes , C. freundii , and H. alvei . Cefepime is generally effective when the MIC is in the susceptible or susceptible-dose-dependent range; ceftriaxone is not suggested for invasive infection with these organisms. 1 HECK-Yes is a memory aid: Hafnia alvei , Enterobacter cloacae complex, Citrobacter freundii , Klebsiella aerogenes , and Yersinia enterocolitica . Approach to a reported penicillin allergy Use the treating institution’s allergy assessment pathway for patient-specific decisions. Start with the history. Document the drug, timing, symptoms, treatment required, time since the reaction, and any beta-lactams tolerated afterward. Most reported penicillin allergies are not confirmed as current IgE-mediated allergy, but an incomplete history should be clarified rather than dismissed. 4 Classify the reaction before choosing another beta-lactam History Typical features Resident action Intolerance or nonallergic history Isolated nausea, diarrhea, headache, family history, or a label entered without a patient reaction. Document the history accurately. These findings alone do not establish immune-mediated allergy. Possible immediate IgE-mediated reaction Urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis beginning within minutes to several hours. Confirm the culprit drug and timing. Follow the local allergy pathway and review side-chain relationships before selecting therapy. Benign delayed eruption Morbilliform or maculopapular rash appearing after several days, without mucosal lesions, blistering, systemic illness, or organ injury. Clarify the phenotype and subsequent tolerance. Selected patients may qualify for supervised challenge under the local pathway. Severe delayed or organ-specific reaction SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, drug-induced liver injury, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or immune thrombocytopenia. Do not use PEN-FAST to clear the allergy or proceed to routine challenge. Avoid the culprit and obtain Allergy/Immunology or specialist guidance. PEN-FAST Scoring F: reaction within 5 years, or timing unknown: 2 points A or S: anaphylaxis or angioedema, or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction: 2 points T: treatment required, or treatment unknown: 1 point Interpretation 0: very low risk, less than 1% 1–2: low risk, about 5% 3: moderate risk, about 20% 4–5: high risk, about 50% Use PEN-FAST as a triage tool, not an order. A score below 3 had a negative predictive value of 96.3% in the original study. 13 The PEN-FAST calculator can help organize the history, but residents should not independently remove the allergy label or order a test dose or oral challenge. Suspected severe delayed reactions follow a separate pathway. Testing, challenge, and desensitization Skin testing Penicillin skin testing evaluates immediate IgE-mediated allergy. It may be followed by an oral amoxicillin challenge. It does not evaluate SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or other serious non-IgE reactions. When to involve Allergy/Immunology Consult when the allergy is forcing clearly inferior therapy, when the patient is likely to need repeated antibiotics because of transplant, chemotherapy, or another immunocompromising condition, or when several antimicrobial allergy labels substantially limit treatment. Graded challenge A graded challenge assesses whether a low-risk patient tolerates the drug. It does not induce temporary tolerance. The eligibility and supervision for a challenge depend on the clinical setting and the evaluating team. Desensitization Desensitization induces temporary tolerance when the preferred drug is required and an appropriate alternative is not available. It requires a supervised protocol and uninterrupted dosing. It is not a routine approach to severe delayed reactions. Cross-reactivity Cross-reactivity is driven mainly by R1 side-chain similarity. For an unverified nonanaphylactic penicillin allergy without a severe delayed phenotype, the 2022 practice parameter supports routine cephalosporin administration without testing or added precautions. A structurally dissimilar cephalosporin such as cefazolin can also be given routinely after penicillin anaphylaxis under the practice parameter. Carbapenem cross-reactivity is very low, and the practice parameter supports carbapenem administration without testing or added precautions after penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, including anaphylaxis. Severe delayed reactions still require separate review. 4 Side-chain relationships worth remembering Index allergy Higher-concern related drug Clinical significance Amoxicillin Cefadroxil These share the same R1 side chain. A convincing immediate amoxicillin reaction deserves specific review before cefadroxil is used. Ampicillin Cephalexin and cefaclor These have identical or closely related amino R1 side chains. Do not treat an ampicillin allergy label as a class-wide cephalosporin ban, but do not ignore the phenotype when choosing one of these drugs. Ceftazidime Aztreonam These share an identical R1 side chain. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime reaction should prompt allergy-guided review before aztreonam. Cefazolin No commonly used beta-lactam shares its R1 side chain An isolated cefazolin allergy does not automatically predict a reaction to penicillins or other cephalosporins. Base the decision on the reaction phenotype. The bedside table above lists the relationships most likely to change a resident's immediate decision. For a complete matrix, see the public Northwestern Medicine cross-reactivity chart . 4 35 41

Beta-lactams Beta-lactams are the backbone of inpatient therapy. For each one, know the usual spectrum and the important gaps. The table assumes a susceptible isolate. ESBL production, AmpC risk, carbapenemases, and local resistance can completely change the answer. Common inpatient beta-lactams Drug Where it is commonly useful Important gaps and cautions Ampicillin or amoxicillin Susceptible streptococci, Enterococcus faecalis , and Listeria . Klebsiella pneumoniae is intrinsically resistant to ampicillin. Activity against E. coli is too variable for routine empiric use. 12 Ampicillin-sulbactam Streptococci, MSSA, susceptible E. faecalis , oral flora, and anaerobes. Commonly used for selected head and neck, aspiration-related, skin, and polymicrobial infections. No Pseudomonas . Empiric E. coli and Klebsiella reliability depends on local susceptibility. CRAB dosing is a separate specialist use. Piperacillin-tazobactam Broad empiric coverage including susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , anaerobes, streptococci, MSSA, and many E. faecalis isolates. No MRSA. Do not assume activity against ESBL or AmpC organisms. It is not preferred definitive therapy for ESBL bloodstream infection. Cefazolin MSSA, streptococci, and susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , and Proteus mirabilis . Often preferred for MSSA infection. No enterococci, MRSA, or Pseudomonas . Not a treatment for ESBL-producing isolates. Ceftriaxone Most streptococci, most pneumococci, and many susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella . Useful for many community-onset infections. No Pseudomonas , enterococci, or MRSA. Avoid as definitive therapy for invasive infection due to organisms at moderate risk of inducible AmpC, including Enterobacter cloacae complex, Klebsiella aerogenes , Citrobacter freundii , and Hafnia alvei . 1 Cefepime Susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , MSSA, and streptococci. Relatively stable against AmpC. No anaerobes, enterococci, or MRSA. Renal adjustment is essential; unexplained encephalopathy or myoclonus should raise concern for neurotoxicity. Ertapenem ESBL-producing E. coli or Klebsiella , susceptible mixed Enterobacterales, and anaerobes when a carbapenem is indicated. No reliable Pseudomonas , Acinetobacter , enterococcal, or MRSA activity. Meropenem Serious ESBL infection, many susceptible Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas , and anaerobes. No MRSA and unreliable enterococcal activity. Preserve for situations where its spectrum or resistance stability is needed. Aztreonam Targeted aerobic gram-negative coverage, including susceptible Pseudomonas , when preferred beta-lactams cannot be used. No gram-positive or anaerobic activity and unreliable empiric coverage for many resistant gram-negative organisms. It is usually a poor empiric monotherapy choice for a seriously ill patient. Avoid routine aztreonam when a better beta-lactam can be given safely. It usually has very low cross-reactivity with other beta-lactams, but it shares an identical R1 side chain with ceftazidime. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime allergy should prompt allergy-guided review rather than routine aztreonam use. 4 21 Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole Where ceftaroline and ceftobiprole fit Drug What makes it different What residents should not assume Ceftaroline Teflaro A cephalosporin with MRSA activity. FDA-labeled uses are acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, including MRSA, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia due to designated susceptible organisms. The pneumonia indication includes MSSA, not MRSA. 22 MRSA bacteremia and endocarditis use is off-label and is supported mainly by observational salvage and combination-therapy experience, not a definitive randomized bacteremia trial. Do not count on Pseudomonas , enterococci, atypical organisms, or clinically adequate anaerobic coverage. Ceftobiprole Zevtera A cephalosporin with activity against MSSA and MRSA. FDA-labeled uses include adult S. aureus bacteremia, including right-sided endocarditis, adult acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia in adults and children at least 3 months old. 23 The bacteremia indication should not be stretched to left-sided endocarditis. It is not a dependable choice for Pseudomonas , ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, anaerobes, or atypical pneumonia pathogens. Confirm formulary status and susceptibility before use. ERADICATE provides randomized trial data for ceftobiprole in complicated S. aureus bacteremia. Ceftobiprole was noninferior to daptomycin for overall treatment success: 69.8% compared with 68.7%. The adjusted difference was 2.0 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from −7.1 to 11.1. Ceftaroline does not have comparable randomized trial evidence for MRSA bacteremia. ERADICATE also should not be extrapolated to every endovascular infection. 24 Consider Klebsiella coverage separately from E. coli . Susceptible isolates may be covered by cefazolin, ceftriaxone, cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a carbapenem, depending on the syndrome and susceptibility result. Ampicillin is not active against K. pneumoniae . A carbapenem is generally preferred for invasive ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae infection. 1 12 Resident essential: ESBL and AmpC are not interchangeable labels ESBL enzymes are most often encountered in E. coli , K. pneumoniae , and K. oxytoca and inactivate most penicillins, cephalosporins, and aztreonam. Carbapenems generally remain active. For organisms at moderate risk of clinically significant inducible AmpC, the 2026 IDSA guidance identifies E. cloacae complex, K. aerogenes , C. freundii , and H. alvei . Cefepime is generally effective when the MIC is in the susceptible or susceptible-dose-dependent range; ceftriaxone is not suggested for invasive infection with these organisms. 1 HECK-Yes is a memory aid: Hafnia alvei , Enterobacter cloacae complex, Citrobacter freundii , Klebsiella aerogenes , and Yersinia enterocolitica . Approach to a reported penicillin allergy Use the treating institution’s allergy assessment pathway for patient-specific decisions. Start with the history. Document the drug, timing, symptoms, treatment required, time since the reaction, and any beta-lactams tolerated afterward. Most reported penicillin allergies are not confirmed as current IgE-mediated allergy, but an incomplete history should be clarified rather than dismissed. 4 Classify the reaction before choosing another beta-lactam History Typical features Resident action Intolerance or nonallergic history Isolated nausea, diarrhea, headache, family history, or a label entered without a patient reaction. Document the history accurately. These findings alone do not establish immune-mediated allergy. Possible immediate IgE-mediated reaction Urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis beginning within minutes to several hours. Confirm the culprit drug and timing. Follow the local allergy pathway and review side-chain relationships before selecting therapy. Benign delayed eruption Morbilliform or maculopapular rash appearing after several days, without mucosal lesions, blistering, systemic illness, or organ injury. Clarify the phenotype and subsequent tolerance. Selected patients may qualify for supervised challenge under the local pathway. Severe delayed or organ-specific reaction SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, drug-induced liver injury, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or immune thrombocytopenia. Do not use PEN-FAST to clear the allergy or proceed to routine challenge. Avoid the culprit and obtain Allergy/Immunology or specialist guidance. PEN-FAST Scoring F: reaction within 5 years, or timing unknown: 2 points A or S: anaphylaxis or angioedema, or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction: 2 points T: treatment required, or treatment unknown: 1 point Interpretation 0: very low risk, less than 1% 1–2: low risk, about 5% 3: moderate risk, about 20% 4–5: high risk, about 50% Use PEN-FAST as a triage tool, not an order. A score below 3 had a negative predictive value of 96.3% in the original study. 13 The PEN-FAST calculator can help organize the history, but residents should not independently remove the allergy label or order a test dose or oral challenge. Suspected severe delayed reactions follow a separate pathway. Testing, challenge, and desensitization Skin testing Penicillin skin testing evaluates immediate IgE-mediated allergy. It may be followed by an oral amoxicillin challenge. It does not evaluate SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or other serious non-IgE reactions. When to involve Allergy/Immunology Consult when the allergy is forcing clearly inferior therapy, when the patient is likely to need repeated antibiotics because of transplant, chemotherapy, or another immunocompromising condition, or when several antimicrobial allergy labels substantially limit treatment. Graded challenge A graded challenge assesses whether a low-risk patient tolerates the drug. It does not induce temporary tolerance. The eligibility and supervision for a challenge depend on the clinical setting and the evaluating team. Desensitization Desensitization induces temporary tolerance when the preferred drug is required and an appropriate alternative is not available. It requires a supervised protocol and uninterrupted dosing. It is not a routine approach to severe delayed reactions. Cross-reactivity Cross-reactivity is driven mainly by R1 side-chain similarity. For an unverified nonanaphylactic penicillin allergy without a severe delayed phenotype, the 2022 practice parameter supports routine cephalosporin administration without testing or added precautions. A structurally dissimilar cephalosporin such as cefazolin can also be given routinely after penicillin anaphylaxis under the practice parameter. Carbapenem cross-reactivity is very low, and the practice parameter supports carbapenem administration without testing or added precautions after penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, including anaphylaxis. Severe delayed reactions still require separate review. 4 Side-chain relationships worth remembering Index allergy Higher-concern related drug Clinical significance Amoxicillin Cefadroxil These share the same R1 side chain. A convincing immediate amoxicillin reaction deserves specific review before cefadroxil is used. Ampicillin Cephalexin and cefaclor These have identical or closely related amino R1 side chains. Do not treat an ampicillin allergy label as a class-wide cephalosporin ban, but do not ignore the phenotype when choosing one of these drugs. Ceftazidime Aztreonam These share an identical R1 side chain. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime reaction should prompt allergy-guided review before aztreonam. Cefazolin No commonly used beta-lactam shares its R1 side chain An isolated cefazolin allergy does not automatically predict a reaction to penicillins or other cephalosporins. Base the decision on the reaction phenotype. The bedside table above lists the relationships most likely to change a resident's immediate decision. For a complete matrix, see the public Northwestern Medicine cross-reactivity chart . 4 35 41

rows: Most streptococci, most pneumococci, and many susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella . Useful for many community-onset infections.

ESBL production, AmpC risk, carbapenemases, and local resistance can completely change the answer. Common inpatient beta-lactams Drug Where it is commonly useful Important gaps and cautions Ampicillin or amoxicillin Susceptible streptococci, Enterococcus faecalis , and Listeria . Klebsiella pneumoniae is intrinsically resistant to ampicillin. Activity against E. coli is too variable for routine empiric use. 12 Ampicillin-sulbactam Streptococci, MSSA, susceptible E. faecalis , oral flora, and anaerobes. Commonly used for selected head and neck, aspiration-related, skin, and polymicrobial infections. No Pseudomonas . Empiric E. coli and Klebsiella reliability depends on local susceptibility. CRAB dosing is a separate specialist use. Piperacillin-tazobactam Broad empiric coverage including susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , anaerobes, streptococci, MSSA, and many E. faecalis isolates. No MRSA. Do not assume activity against ESBL or AmpC organisms. It is not preferred definitive therapy for ESBL bloodstream infection. Cefazolin MSSA, streptococci, and susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , and Proteus mirabilis . Often preferred for MSSA infection. No enterococci, MRSA, or Pseudomonas . Not a treatment for ESBL-producing isolates. Ceftriaxone Most streptococci, most pneumococci, and many susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella . Useful for many community-onset infections. No Pseudomonas , enterococci, or MRSA. Avoid as definitive therapy for invasive infection due to organisms at moderate risk of inducible AmpC, including Enterobacter cloacae complex, Klebsiella aerogenes , Citrobacter freundii , and Hafnia alvei . 1 Cefepime Susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , MSSA, and streptococci. Relatively stable against AmpC. No anaerobes, enterococci, or MRSA. Renal adjustment is essential; unexplained encephalopathy or myoclonus should raise concern for neurotoxicity. Ertapenem ESBL-producing E. coli or Klebsiella , susceptible mixed Enterobacterales, and anaerobes when a carbapenem is indicated. No reliable Pseudomonas , Acinetobacter , enterococcal, or MRSA activity. Meropenem Serious ESBL infection, many susceptible Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas , and anaerobes. No MRSA and unreliable enterococcal activity. Preserve for situations where its spectrum or resistance stability is needed. Aztreonam Targeted aerobic gram-negative coverage, including susceptible Pseudomonas , when preferred beta-lactams cannot be used. No gram-positive or anaerobic activity and unreliable empiric coverage for many resistant gram-negative organisms. It is usually a poor empiric monotherapy choice for a seriously ill patient. Avoid routine aztreonam when a better beta-lactam can be given safely. It usually has very low cross-reactivity with other beta-lactams, but it shares an identical R1 side chain with ceftazidime. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime allergy should prompt allergy-guided review rather than routine aztreonam use. 4 21 Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole Where ceftaroline and ceftobiprole fit Drug What makes it different What residents should not assume Ceftaroline Teflaro A cephalosporin with MRSA activity. FDA-labeled uses are acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, including MRSA, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia due to designated susceptible organisms. The pneumonia indication includes MSSA, not MRSA. 22 MRSA bacteremia and endocarditis use is off-label and is supported mainly by observational salvage and combination-therapy experience, not a definitive randomized bacteremia trial. Do not count on Pseudomonas , enterococci, atypical organisms, or clinically adequate anaerobic coverage. Ceftobiprole Zevtera A cephalosporin with activity against MSSA and MRSA. FDA-labeled uses include adult S. aureus bacteremia, including right-sided endocarditis, adult acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia in adults and children at least 3 months old. 23 The bacteremia indication should not be stretched to left-sided endocarditis. It is not a dependable choice for Pseudomonas , ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, anaerobes, or atypical pneumonia pathogens. Confirm formulary status and susceptibility before use. ERADICATE provides randomized trial data for ceftobiprole in complicated S. aureus bacteremia. Ceftobiprole was noninferior to daptomycin for overall treatment success: 69.8% compared with 68.7%. The adjusted difference was 2.0 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from −7.1 to 11.1. Ceftaroline does not have comparable randomized trial evidence for MRSA bacteremia. Susceptible isolates may be covered by cefazolin, ceftriaxone, cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a carbapenem, depending on the syndrome and susceptibility result. For organisms at moderate risk of clinically significant inducible AmpC, the 2026 IDSA guidance identifies E. cloacae complex, K. aerogenes , C. freundii , and H. alvei . Approach to a reported penicillin allergy Use the treating institution’s allergy assessment pathway for patient-specific decisions. Start with the history. Document the drug, timing, symptoms, treatment required, time since the reaction, and any beta-lactams tolerated afterward. Most reported penicillin allergies are not confirmed as current IgE-mediated allergy, but an incomplete history should be clarified rather than dismissed. 4 Classify the reaction before choosing another beta-lactam History Typical features Resident action Intolerance or nonallergic history Isolated nausea, diarrhea, headache, family history, or a label entered without a patient reaction. Document the history accurately. These findings alone do not establish immune-mediated allergy. Possible immediate IgE-mediated reaction Urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis beginning within minutes to several hours. Confirm the culprit drug and timing. Follow the local allergy pathway and review side-chain relationships before selecting therapy. Benign delayed eruption Morbilliform or maculopapular rash appearing after several days, without mucosal lesions, blistering, systemic illness, or organ injury. Clarify the phenotype and subsequent tolerance. Selected patients may qualify for supervised challenge under the local pathway. Severe delayed or organ-specific reaction SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, drug-induced liver injury, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or immune thrombocytopenia. Do not use PEN-FAST to clear the allergy or proceed to routine challenge. Avoid the culprit and obtain Allergy/Immunology or specialist guidance. PEN-FAST Scoring F: reaction within 5 years, or timing unknown: 2 points A or S: anaphylaxis or angioedema, or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction: 2 points T: treatment required, or treatment unknown: 1 point Interpretation 0: very low risk, less than 1% 1–2: low risk, about 5% 3: moderate risk, about 20% 4–5: high risk, about 50% Use PEN-FAST as a triage tool, not an order. Suspected severe delayed reactions follow a separate pathway. Testing, challenge, and desensitization Skin testing Penicillin skin testing evaluates immediate IgE-mediated allergy. It may be followed by an oral amoxicillin challenge. It does not evaluate SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or other serious non-IgE reactions. When to involve Allergy/Immunology Consult when the allergy is forcing clearly inferior therapy, when the patient is likely to need repeated antibiotics because of transplant, chemotherapy, or another immunocompromising condition, or when several antimicrobial allergy labels substantially limit treatment. Graded challenge A graded challenge assesses whether a low-risk patient tolerates the drug. It does not induce temporary tolerance. The eligibility and supervision for a challenge depend on the clinical setting and the evaluating team. Desensitization Desensitization induces temporary tolerance when the preferred drug is required and an appropriate alternative is not available. It requires a supervised protocol and uninterrupted dosing. It is not a routine approach to severe delayed reactions. Cross-reactivity Cross-reactivity is driven mainly by R1 side-chain similarity. For an unverified nonanaphylactic penicillin allergy without a severe delayed phenotype, the 2022 practice parameter supports routine cephalosporin administration without testing or added precautions. A structurally dissimilar cephalosporin such as cefazolin can also be given routinely after penicillin anaphylaxis under the practice parameter. Carbapenem cross-reactivity is very low, and the practice parameter supports carbapenem administration without testing or added precautions after penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, including anaphylaxis. Severe delayed reactions still require separate review. 4 Side-chain relationships worth remembering Index allergy Higher-concern related drug Clinical significance Amoxicillin Cefadroxil These share the same R1 side chain. A convincing immediate amoxicillin reaction deserves specific review before cefadroxil is used. Ampicillin Cephalexin and cefaclor These have identical or closely related amino R1 side chains. Do not treat an ampicillin allergy label as a class-wide cephalosporin ban, but do not ignore the phenotype when choosing one of these drugs. Ceftazidime Aztreonam These share an identical R1 side chain. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime reaction should prompt allergy-guided review before aztreonam. Cefazolin No commonly used beta-lactam shares its R1 side chain An isolated cefazolin allergy does not automatically predict a reaction to penicillins or other cephalosporins. Base the decision on the reaction phenotype. The bedside table above lists the relationships most likely to change a resident's immediate decision. For a complete matrix, see the public Northwestern Medicine cross-reactivity chart . 4 35 41

rows: ESBL-producing E. coli or Klebsiella , susceptible mixed Enterobacterales, and anaerobes when a carbapenem is indicated.
No reliable Pseudomonas , Acinetobacter , enterococcal, or MRSA activity.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Beta-lactams Beta-lactams are the backbone of inpatient therapy. For each one, know the usual spectrum and the important gaps. The table assumes a susceptible isolate. ESBL production, AmpC risk, carbapenemases, and local resistance can completely change the answer. Common inpatient beta-lactams Drug Where it is commonly useful Important gaps and cautions Ampicillin or amoxicillin Susceptible streptococci, Enterococcus faecalis , and Listeria . Klebsiella pneumoniae is intrinsically resistant to ampicillin. Activity against E. coli is too variable for routine empiric use. 12 Ampicillin-sulbactam Streptococci, MSSA, susceptible E. faecalis , oral flora, and anaerobes. Commonly used for selected head and neck, aspiration-related, skin, and polymicrobial infections. No Pseudomonas . Empiric E. coli and Klebsiella reliability depends on local susceptibility. CRAB dosing is a separate specialist use. Piperacillin-tazobactam Broad empiric coverage including susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , anaerobes, streptococci, MSSA, and many E. faecalis isolates. No MRSA. Do not assume activity against ESBL or AmpC organisms. It is not preferred definitive therapy for ESBL bloodstream infection. Cefazolin MSSA, streptococci, and susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , and Proteus mirabilis . Often preferred for MSSA infection. No enterococci, MRSA, or Pseudomonas . Not a treatment for ESBL-producing isolates. Ceftriaxone Most streptococci, most pneumococci, and many susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella . Useful for many community-onset infections. No Pseudomonas , enterococci, or MRSA. Avoid as definitive therapy for invasive infection due to organisms at moderate risk of inducible AmpC, including Enterobacter cloacae complex, Klebsiella aerogenes , Citrobacter freundii , and Hafnia alvei . 1 Cefepime Susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , MSSA, and streptococci. Relatively stable against AmpC. No anaerobes, enterococci, or MRSA. Renal adjustment is essential; unexplained encephalopathy or myoclonus should raise concern for neurotoxicity. Ertapenem ESBL-producing E. coli or Klebsiella , susceptible mixed Enterobacterales, and anaerobes when a carbapenem is indicated. No reliable Pseudomonas , Acinetobacter , enterococcal, or MRSA activity. Meropenem Serious ESBL infection, many susceptible Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas , and anaerobes. No MRSA and unreliable enterococcal activity. Preserve for situations where its spectrum or resistance stability is needed. Aztreonam Targeted aerobic gram-negative coverage, including susceptible Pseudomonas , when preferred beta-lactams cannot be used. No gram-positive or anaerobic activity and unreliable empiric coverage for many resistant gram-negative organisms. It is usually a poor empiric monotherapy choice for a seriously ill patient. Avoid routine aztreonam when a better beta-lactam can be given safely. It usually has very low cross-reactivity with other beta-lactams, but it shares an identical R1 side chain with ceftazidime. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime allergy should prompt allergy-guided review rather than routine aztreonam use. 4 21 Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole Where ceftaroline and ceftobiprole fit Drug What makes it different What residents should not assume Ceftaroline Teflaro A cephalosporin with MRSA activity. FDA-labeled uses are acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, including MRSA, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia due to designated susceptible organisms. The pneumonia indication includes MSSA, not MRSA. 22 MRSA bacteremia and endocarditis use is off-label and is supported mainly by observational salvage and combination-therapy experience, not a definitive randomized bacteremia trial. Do not count on Pseudomonas , enterococci, atypical organisms, or clinically adequate anaerobic coverage. Ceftobiprole Zevtera A cephalosporin with activity against MSSA and MRSA. FDA-labeled uses include adult S. aureus bacteremia, including right-sided endocarditis, adult acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia in adults and children at least 3 months old. 23 The bacteremia indication should not be stretched to left-sided endocarditis. It is not a dependable choice for Pseudomonas , ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, anaerobes, or atypical pneumonia pathogens. Confirm formulary status and susceptibility before use. ERADICATE provides randomized trial data for ceftobiprole in complicated S. aureus bacteremia. Ceftobiprole was noninferior to daptomycin for overall treatment success: 69.8% compared with 68.7%. The adjusted difference was 2.0 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from −7.1 to 11.1. Ceftaroline does not have comparable randomized trial evidence for MRSA bacteremia. ERADICATE also should not be extrapolated to every endovascular infection. 24 Consider Klebsiella coverage separately from E. coli . Susceptible isolates may be covered by cefazolin, ceftriaxone, cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a carbapenem, depending on the syndrome and susceptibility result. Ampicillin is not active against K. pneumoniae . A carbapenem is generally preferred for invasive ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae infection. 1 12 Resident essential: ESBL and AmpC are not interchangeable labels ESBL enzymes are most often encountered in E. coli , K. pneumoniae , and K. oxytoca and inactivate most penicillins, cephalosporins, and aztreonam. Carbapenems generally remain active. For organisms at moderate risk of clinically significant inducible AmpC, the 2026 IDSA guidance identifies E. cloacae complex, K. aerogenes , C. freundii , and H. alvei . Cefepime is generally effective when the MIC is in the susceptible or susceptible-dose-dependent range; ceftriaxone is not suggested for invasive infection with these organisms. 1 HECK-Yes is a memory aid: Hafnia alvei , Enterobacter cloacae complex, Citrobacter freundii , Klebsiella aerogenes , and Yersinia enterocolitica . Approach to a reported penicillin allergy Use the treating institution’s allergy assessment pathway for patient-specific decisions. Start with the history. Document the drug, timing, symptoms, treatment required, time since the reaction, and any beta-lactams tolerated afterward. Most reported penicillin allergies are not confirmed as current IgE-mediated allergy, but an incomplete history should be clarified rather than dismissed. 4 Classify the reaction before choosing another beta-lactam History Typical features Resident action Intolerance or nonallergic history Isolated nausea, diarrhea, headache, family history, or a label entered without a patient reaction. Document the history accurately. These findings alone do not establish immune-mediated allergy. Possible immediate IgE-mediated reaction Urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis beginning within minutes to several hours. Confirm the culprit drug and timing. Follow the local allergy pathway and review side-chain relationships before selecting therapy. Benign delayed eruption Morbilliform or maculopapular rash appearing after several days, without mucosal lesions, blistering, systemic illness, or organ injury. Clarify the phenotype and subsequent tolerance. Selected patients may qualify for supervised challenge under the local pathway. Severe delayed or organ-specific reaction SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, drug-induced liver injury, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or immune thrombocytopenia. Do not use PEN-FAST to clear the allergy or proceed to routine challenge. Avoid the culprit and obtain Allergy/Immunology or specialist guidance. PEN-FAST Scoring F: reaction within 5 years, or timing unknown: 2 points A or S: anaphylaxis or angioedema, or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction: 2 points T: treatment required, or treatment unknown: 1 point Interpretation 0: very low risk, less than 1% 1–2: low risk, about 5% 3: moderate risk, about 20% 4–5: high risk, about 50% Use PEN-FAST as a triage tool, not an order. A score below 3 had a negative predictive value of 96.3% in the original study. 13 The PEN-FAST calculator can help organize the history, but residents should not independently remove the allergy label or order a test dose or oral challenge. Suspected severe delayed reactions follow a separate pathway. Testing, challenge, and desensitization Skin testing Penicillin skin testing evaluates immediate IgE-mediated allergy. It may be followed by an oral amoxicillin challenge. It does not evaluate SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or other serious non-IgE reactions. When to involve Allergy/Immunology Consult when the allergy is forcing clearly inferior therapy, when the patient is likely to need repeated antibiotics because of transplant, chemotherapy, or another immunocompromising condition, or when several antimicrobial allergy labels substantially limit treatment. Graded challenge A graded challenge assesses whether a low-risk patient tolerates the drug. It does not induce temporary tolerance. The eligibility and supervision for a challenge depend on the clinical setting and the evaluating team. Desensitization Desensitization induces temporary tolerance when the preferred drug is required and an appropriate alternative is not available. It requires a supervised protocol and uninterrupted dosing. It is not a routine approach to severe delayed reactions. Cross-reactivity Cross-reactivity is driven mainly by R1 side-chain similarity. For an unverified nonanaphylactic penicillin allergy without a severe delayed phenotype, the 2022 practice parameter supports routine cephalosporin administration without testing or added precautions. A structurally dissimilar cephalosporin such as cefazolin can also be given routinely after penicillin anaphylaxis under the practice parameter. Carbapenem cross-reactivity is very low, and the practice parameter supports carbapenem administration without testing or added precautions after penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, including anaphylaxis. Severe delayed reactions still require separate review. 4 Side-chain relationships worth remembering Index allergy Higher-concern related drug Clinical significance Amoxicillin Cefadroxil These share the same R1 side chain. A convincing immediate amoxicillin reaction deserves specific review before cefadroxil is used. Ampicillin Cephalexin and cefaclor These have identical or closely related amino R1 side chains. Do not treat an ampicillin allergy label as a class-wide cephalosporin ban, but do not ignore the phenotype when choosing one of these drugs. Ceftazidime Aztreonam These share an identical R1 side chain. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime reaction should prompt allergy-guided review before aztreonam. Cefazolin No commonly used beta-lactam shares its R1 side chain An isolated cefazolin allergy does not automatically predict a reaction to penicillins or other cephalosporins. Base the decision on the reaction phenotype. The bedside table above lists the relationships most likely to change a resident's immediate decision. For a complete matrix, see the public Northwestern Medicine cross-reactivity chart . 4 35 41

ESBL production, AmpC risk, carbapenemases, and local resistance can completely change the answer. Klebsiella pneumoniae is intrinsically resistant to ampicillin. Activity against E. coli is too variable for routine empiric use. 12 Ampicillin-sulbactam Streptococci, MSSA, susceptible E. faecalis , oral flora, and anaerobes. Commonly used for selected head and neck, aspiration-related, skin, and polymicrobial infections. No Pseudomonas . Empiric E. coli and Klebsiella reliability depends on local susceptibility. CRAB dosing is a separate specialist use. Piperacillin-tazobactam Broad empiric coverage including susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , anaerobes, streptococci, MSSA, and many E. faecalis isolates. No MRSA. Do not assume activity against ESBL or AmpC organisms. It is not preferred definitive therapy for ESBL bloodstream infection. Cefazolin MSSA, streptococci, and susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , and Proteus mirabilis . Often preferred for MSSA infection. No enterococci, MRSA, or Pseudomonas . Not a treatment for ESBL-producing isolates. Ceftriaxone Most streptococci, most pneumococci, and many susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella . Useful for many community-onset infections. No Pseudomonas , enterococci, or MRSA. Relatively stable against AmpC. No anaerobes, enterococci, or MRSA. Renal adjustment is essential; unexplained encephalopathy or myoclonus should raise concern for neurotoxicity. Ertapenem ESBL-producing E. coli or Klebsiella , susceptible mixed Enterobacterales, and anaerobes when a carbapenem is indicated. No reliable Pseudomonas , Acinetobacter , enterococcal, or MRSA activity. Meropenem Serious ESBL infection, many susceptible Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas , and anaerobes. No MRSA and unreliable enterococcal activity. Preserve for situations where its spectrum or resistance stability is needed. Aztreonam Targeted aerobic gram-negative coverage, including susceptible Pseudomonas , when preferred beta-lactams cannot be used. No gram-positive or anaerobic activity and unreliable empiric coverage for many resistant gram-negative organisms. It is usually a poor empiric monotherapy choice for a seriously ill patient. Avoid routine aztreonam when a better beta-lactam can be given safely. It usually has very low cross-reactivity with other beta-lactams, but it shares an identical R1 side chain with ceftazidime. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime allergy should prompt allergy-guided review rather than routine aztreonam use. 4 21 Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole Where ceftaroline and ceftobiprole fit Drug What makes it different What residents should not assume Ceftaroline Teflaro A cephalosporin with MRSA activity. FDA-labeled uses are acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, including MRSA, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia due to designated susceptible organisms. The pneumonia indication includes MSSA, not MRSA. 22 MRSA bacteremia and endocarditis use is off-label and is supported mainly by observational salvage and combination-therapy experience, not a definitive randomized bacteremia trial. Do not count on Pseudomonas , enterococci, atypical organisms, or clinically adequate anaerobic coverage. Ceftobiprole Zevtera A cephalosporin with activity against MSSA and MRSA. FDA-labeled uses include adult S. aureus bacteremia, including right-sided endocarditis, adult acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia in adults and children at least 3 months old. 23 The bacteremia indication should not be stretched to left-sided endocarditis. It is not a dependable choice for Pseudomonas , ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, anaerobes, or atypical pneumonia pathogens. Confirm formulary status and susceptibility before use. Graded challenge A graded challenge assesses whether a low-risk patient tolerates the drug. It does not induce temporary tolerance. The eligibility and supervision for a challenge depend on the clinical setting and the evaluating team. Desensitization Desensitization induces temporary tolerance when the preferred drug is required and an appropriate alternative is not available. It requires a supervised protocol and uninterrupted dosing. It is not a routine approach to severe delayed reactions. Cross-reactivity Cross-reactivity is driven mainly by R1 side-chain similarity. For an unverified nonanaphylactic penicillin allergy without a severe delayed phenotype, the 2022 practice parameter supports routine cephalosporin administration without testing or added precautions. Ceftazidime Aztreonam These share an identical R1 side chain. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime reaction should prompt allergy-guided review before aztreonam. Cefazolin No commonly used beta-lactam shares its R1 side chain An isolated cefazolin allergy does not automatically predict a reaction to penicillins or other cephalosporins. slides.title: Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole
paragraphs: ERADICATE provides randomized trial data for ceftobiprole in complicated S. aureus bacteremia. Ceftobiprole was noninferior to daptomycin for overall treatment success: 69.8% compared with 68.7%. The adjusted difference was 2.0 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from −7.1 to 11.1. Ceftaroline does not have comparable randomized trial evidence for MRSA bacteremia. ERADICATE also should not be extrapolated to every endovascular infection. 24

Not a treatment for ESBL-producing isolates. Ceftriaxone Most streptococci, most pneumococci, and many susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella . Useful for many community-onset infections. No Pseudomonas , enterococci, or MRSA. Document the drug, timing, symptoms, treatment required, time since the reaction, and any beta-lactams tolerated afterward. Most reported penicillin allergies are not confirmed as current IgE-mediated allergy, but an incomplete history should be clarified rather than dismissed. 4 Classify the reaction before choosing another beta-lactam History Typical features Resident action Intolerance or nonallergic history Isolated nausea, diarrhea, headache, family history, or a label entered without a patient reaction. Document the history accurately. These findings alone do not establish immune-mediated allergy. Clarify the phenotype and subsequent tolerance. Selected patients may qualify for supervised challenge under the local pathway. Ceftazidime Aztreonam These share an identical R1 side chain. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime reaction should prompt allergy-guided review before aztreonam. Cefazolin No commonly used beta-lactam shares its R1 side chain An isolated cefazolin allergy does not automatically predict a reaction to penicillins or other cephalosporins. Base the decision on the reaction phenotype. The bedside table above lists the relationships most likely to change a resident's immediate decision. For a complete matrix, see the public Northwestern Medicine cross-reactivity chart . 4 35 41

slides.title: Resident essential: ESBL and AmpC are not interchangeable labels
paragraphs: ESBL enzymes are most often encountered in E. coli , K. pneumoniae , and K. oxytoca and inactivate most penicillins, cephalosporins, and aztreonam. Carbapenems generally remain active. For organisms at moderate risk of clinically significant inducible AmpC, the 2026 IDSA guidance identifies E. cloacae complex, K. aerogenes , C. freundii , and H. alvei . Cefepime is generally effective when the MIC is in the susceptible or susceptible-dose-dependent range; ceftriaxone is not suggested for invasive infection with these organisms. 1
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Beta-lactams Beta-lactams are the backbone of inpatient therapy. For each one, know the usual spectrum and the important gaps. The table assumes a susceptible isolate. ESBL production, AmpC risk, carbapenemases, and local resistance can completely change the answer. Common inpatient beta-lactams Drug Where it is commonly useful Important gaps and cautions Ampicillin or amoxicillin Susceptible streptococci, Enterococcus faecalis , and Listeria . Klebsiella pneumoniae is intrinsically resistant to ampicillin. Activity against E. coli is too variable for routine empiric use. 12 Ampicillin-sulbactam Streptococci, MSSA, susceptible E. faecalis , oral flora, and anaerobes. Commonly used for selected head and neck, aspiration-related, skin, and polymicrobial infections. No Pseudomonas . Empiric E. coli and Klebsiella reliability depends on local susceptibility. CRAB dosing is a separate specialist use. Piperacillin-tazobactam Broad empiric coverage including susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , anaerobes, streptococci, MSSA, and many E. faecalis isolates. No MRSA. Do not assume activity against ESBL or AmpC organisms. It is not preferred definitive therapy for ESBL bloodstream infection. Cefazolin MSSA, streptococci, and susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , and Proteus mirabilis . Often preferred for MSSA infection. No enterococci, MRSA, or Pseudomonas . Not a treatment for ESBL-producing isolates. Ceftriaxone Most streptococci, most pneumococci, and many susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella . Useful for many community-onset infections. No Pseudomonas , enterococci, or MRSA. Avoid as definitive therapy for invasive infection due to organisms at moderate risk of inducible AmpC, including Enterobacter cloacae complex, Klebsiella aerogenes , Citrobacter freundii , and Hafnia alvei . 1 Cefepime Susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , MSSA, and streptococci. Relatively stable against AmpC. No anaerobes, enterococci, or MRSA. Renal adjustment is essential; unexplained encephalopathy or myoclonus should raise concern for neurotoxicity. Ertapenem ESBL-producing E. coli or Klebsiella , susceptible mixed Enterobacterales, and anaerobes when a carbapenem is indicated. No reliable Pseudomonas , Acinetobacter , enterococcal, or MRSA activity. Meropenem Serious ESBL infection, many susceptible Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas , and anaerobes. No MRSA and unreliable enterococcal activity. Preserve for situations where its spectrum or resistance stability is needed. Aztreonam Targeted aerobic gram-negative coverage, including susceptible Pseudomonas , when preferred beta-lactams cannot be used. No gram-positive or anaerobic activity and unreliable empiric coverage for many resistant gram-negative organisms. It is usually a poor empiric monotherapy choice for a seriously ill patient. Avoid routine aztreonam when a better beta-lactam can be given safely. It usually has very low cross-reactivity with other beta-lactams, but it shares an identical R1 side chain with ceftazidime. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime allergy should prompt allergy-guided review rather than routine aztreonam use. 4 21 Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole Where ceftaroline and ceftobiprole fit Drug What makes it different What residents should not assume Ceftaroline Teflaro A cephalosporin with MRSA activity. FDA-labeled uses are acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, including MRSA, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia due to designated susceptible organisms. The pneumonia indication includes MSSA, not MRSA. 22 MRSA bacteremia and endocarditis use is off-label and is supported mainly by observational salvage and combination-therapy experience, not a definitive randomized bacteremia trial. Do not count on Pseudomonas , enterococci, atypical organisms, or clinically adequate anaerobic coverage. Ceftobiprole Zevtera A cephalosporin with activity against MSSA and MRSA. FDA-labeled uses include adult S. aureus bacteremia, including right-sided endocarditis, adult acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia in adults and children at least 3 months old. 23 The bacteremia indication should not be stretched to left-sided endocarditis. It is not a dependable choice for Pseudomonas , ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, anaerobes, or atypical pneumonia pathogens. Confirm formulary status and susceptibility before use. ERADICATE provides randomized trial data for ceftobiprole in complicated S. aureus bacteremia. Ceftobiprole was noninferior to daptomycin for overall treatment success: 69.8% compared with 68.7%. The adjusted difference was 2.0 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from −7.1 to 11.1. Ceftaroline does not have comparable randomized trial evidence for MRSA bacteremia. ERADICATE also should not be extrapolated to every endovascular infection. 24 Consider Klebsiella coverage separately from E. coli . Susceptible isolates may be covered by cefazolin, ceftriaxone, cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a carbapenem, depending on the syndrome and susceptibility result. Ampicillin is not active against K. pneumoniae . A carbapenem is generally preferred for invasive ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae infection. 1 12 Resident essential: ESBL and AmpC are not interchangeable labels ESBL enzymes are most often encountered in E. coli , K. pneumoniae , and K. oxytoca and inactivate most penicillins, cephalosporins, and aztreonam. Carbapenems generally remain active. For organisms at moderate risk of clinically significant inducible AmpC, the 2026 IDSA guidance identifies E. cloacae complex, K. aerogenes , C. freundii , and H. alvei . Cefepime is generally effective when the MIC is in the susceptible or susceptible-dose-dependent range; ceftriaxone is not suggested for invasive infection with these organisms. 1 HECK-Yes is a memory aid: Hafnia alvei , Enterobacter cloacae complex, Citrobacter freundii , Klebsiella aerogenes , and Yersinia enterocolitica . Approach to a reported penicillin allergy Use the treating institution’s allergy assessment pathway for patient-specific decisions. Start with the history. Document the drug, timing, symptoms, treatment required, time since the reaction, and any beta-lactams tolerated afterward. Most reported penicillin allergies are not confirmed as current IgE-mediated allergy, but an incomplete history should be clarified rather than dismissed. 4 Classify the reaction before choosing another beta-lactam History Typical features Resident action Intolerance or nonallergic history Isolated nausea, diarrhea, headache, family history, or a label entered without a patient reaction. Document the history accurately. These findings alone do not establish immune-mediated allergy. Possible immediate IgE-mediated reaction Urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis beginning within minutes to several hours. Confirm the culprit drug and timing. Follow the local allergy pathway and review side-chain relationships before selecting therapy. Benign delayed eruption Morbilliform or maculopapular rash appearing after several days, without mucosal lesions, blistering, systemic illness, or organ injury. Clarify the phenotype and subsequent tolerance. Selected patients may qualify for supervised challenge under the local pathway. Severe delayed or organ-specific reaction SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, drug-induced liver injury, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or immune thrombocytopenia. Do not use PEN-FAST to clear the allergy or proceed to routine challenge. Avoid the culprit and obtain Allergy/Immunology or specialist guidance. PEN-FAST Scoring F: reaction within 5 years, or timing unknown: 2 points A or S: anaphylaxis or angioedema, or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction: 2 points T: treatment required, or treatment unknown: 1 point Interpretation 0: very low risk, less than 1% 1–2: low risk, about 5% 3: moderate risk, about 20% 4–5: high risk, about 50% Use PEN-FAST as a triage tool, not an order. A score below 3 had a negative predictive value of 96.3% in the original study. 13 The PEN-FAST calculator can help organize the history, but residents should not independently remove the allergy label or order a test dose or oral challenge. Suspected severe delayed reactions follow a separate pathway. Testing, challenge, and desensitization Skin testing Penicillin skin testing evaluates immediate IgE-mediated allergy. It may be followed by an oral amoxicillin challenge. It does not evaluate SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or other serious non-IgE reactions. When to involve Allergy/Immunology Consult when the allergy is forcing clearly inferior therapy, when the patient is likely to need repeated antibiotics because of transplant, chemotherapy, or another immunocompromising condition, or when several antimicrobial allergy labels substantially limit treatment. Graded challenge A graded challenge assesses whether a low-risk patient tolerates the drug. It does not induce temporary tolerance. The eligibility and supervision for a challenge depend on the clinical setting and the evaluating team. Desensitization Desensitization induces temporary tolerance when the preferred drug is required and an appropriate alternative is not available. It requires a supervised protocol and uninterrupted dosing. It is not a routine approach to severe delayed reactions. Cross-reactivity Cross-reactivity is driven mainly by R1 side-chain similarity. For an unverified nonanaphylactic penicillin allergy without a severe delayed phenotype, the 2022 practice parameter supports routine cephalosporin administration without testing or added precautions. A structurally dissimilar cephalosporin such as cefazolin can also be given routinely after penicillin anaphylaxis under the practice parameter. Carbapenem cross-reactivity is very low, and the practice parameter supports carbapenem administration without testing or added precautions after penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, including anaphylaxis. Severe delayed reactions still require separate review. 4 Side-chain relationships worth remembering Index allergy Higher-concern related drug Clinical significance Amoxicillin Cefadroxil These share the same R1 side chain. A convincing immediate amoxicillin reaction deserves specific review before cefadroxil is used. Ampicillin Cephalexin and cefaclor These have identical or closely related amino R1 side chains. Do not treat an ampicillin allergy label as a class-wide cephalosporin ban, but do not ignore the phenotype when choosing one of these drugs. Ceftazidime Aztreonam These share an identical R1 side chain. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime reaction should prompt allergy-guided review before aztreonam. Cefazolin No commonly used beta-lactam shares its R1 side chain An isolated cefazolin allergy does not automatically predict a reaction to penicillins or other cephalosporins. Base the decision on the reaction phenotype. The bedside table above lists the relationships most likely to change a resident's immediate decision. For a complete matrix, see the public Northwestern Medicine cross-reactivity chart . 4 35 41

slides.title: Approach to a reported penicillin allergy
paragraphs: Use the treating institution’s allergy assessment pathway for patient-specific decisions.

Start with the history. Document the drug, timing, symptoms, treatment required, time since the reaction, and any beta-lactams tolerated afterward. Most reported penicillin allergies are not confirmed as current IgE-mediated allergy, but an incomplete history should be clarified rather than dismissed. 4

Complete source section:
Beta-lactams Beta-lactams are the backbone of inpatient therapy. For each one, know the usual spectrum and the important gaps. The table assumes a susceptible isolate. ESBL production, AmpC risk, carbapenemases, and local resistance can completely change the answer. Common inpatient beta-lactams Drug Where it is commonly useful Important gaps and cautions Ampicillin or amoxicillin Susceptible streptococci, Enterococcus faecalis , and Listeria . Klebsiella pneumoniae is intrinsically resistant to ampicillin. Activity against E. coli is too variable for routine empiric use. 12 Ampicillin-sulbactam Streptococci, MSSA, susceptible E. faecalis , oral flora, and anaerobes. Commonly used for selected head and neck, aspiration-related, skin, and polymicrobial infections. No Pseudomonas . Empiric E. coli and Klebsiella reliability depends on local susceptibility. CRAB dosing is a separate specialist use. Piperacillin-tazobactam Broad empiric coverage including susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , anaerobes, streptococci, MSSA, and many E. faecalis isolates. No MRSA. Do not assume activity against ESBL or AmpC organisms. It is not preferred definitive therapy for ESBL bloodstream infection. Cefazolin MSSA, streptococci, and susceptible E. coli , Klebsiella , and Proteus mirabilis . Often preferred for MSSA infection. No enterococci, MRSA, or Pseudomonas . Not a treatment for ESBL-producing isolates. Ceftriaxone Most streptococci, most pneumococci, and many susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella . Useful for many community-onset infections. No Pseudomonas , enterococci, or MRSA. Avoid as definitive therapy for invasive infection due to organisms at moderate risk of inducible AmpC, including Enterobacter cloacae complex, Klebsiella aerogenes , Citrobacter freundii , and Hafnia alvei . 1 Cefepime Susceptible Enterobacterales, including E. coli and Klebsiella , Pseudomonas , MSSA, and streptococci. Relatively stable against AmpC. No anaerobes, enterococci, or MRSA. Renal adjustment is essential; unexplained encephalopathy or myoclonus should raise concern for neurotoxicity. Ertapenem ESBL-producing E. coli or Klebsiella , susceptible mixed Enterobacterales, and anaerobes when a carbapenem is indicated. No reliable Pseudomonas , Acinetobacter , enterococcal, or MRSA activity. Meropenem Serious ESBL infection, many susceptible Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas , and anaerobes. No MRSA and unreliable enterococcal activity. Preserve for situations where its spectrum or resistance stability is needed. Aztreonam Targeted aerobic gram-negative coverage, including susceptible Pseudomonas , when preferred beta-lactams cannot be used. No gram-positive or anaerobic activity and unreliable empiric coverage for many resistant gram-negative organisms. It is usually a poor empiric monotherapy choice for a seriously ill patient. Avoid routine aztreonam when a better beta-lactam can be given safely. It usually has very low cross-reactivity with other beta-lactams, but it shares an identical R1 side chain with ceftazidime. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime allergy should prompt allergy-guided review rather than routine aztreonam use. 4 21 Ceftaroline and ceftobiprole Where ceftaroline and ceftobiprole fit Drug What makes it different What residents should not assume Ceftaroline Teflaro A cephalosporin with MRSA activity. FDA-labeled uses are acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, including MRSA, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia due to designated susceptible organisms. The pneumonia indication includes MSSA, not MRSA. 22 MRSA bacteremia and endocarditis use is off-label and is supported mainly by observational salvage and combination-therapy experience, not a definitive randomized bacteremia trial. Do not count on Pseudomonas , enterococci, atypical organisms, or clinically adequate anaerobic coverage. Ceftobiprole Zevtera A cephalosporin with activity against MSSA and MRSA. FDA-labeled uses include adult S. aureus bacteremia, including right-sided endocarditis, adult acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infection, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia in adults and children at least 3 months old. 23 The bacteremia indication should not be stretched to left-sided endocarditis. It is not a dependable choice for Pseudomonas , ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, anaerobes, or atypical pneumonia pathogens. Confirm formulary status and susceptibility before use. ERADICATE provides randomized trial data for ceftobiprole in complicated S. aureus bacteremia. Ceftobiprole was noninferior to daptomycin for overall treatment success: 69.8% compared with 68.7%. The adjusted difference was 2.0 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from −7.1 to 11.1. Ceftaroline does not have comparable randomized trial evidence for MRSA bacteremia. ERADICATE also should not be extrapolated to every endovascular infection. 24 Consider Klebsiella coverage separately from E. coli . Susceptible isolates may be covered by cefazolin, ceftriaxone, cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or a carbapenem, depending on the syndrome and susceptibility result. Ampicillin is not active against K. pneumoniae . A carbapenem is generally preferred for invasive ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae infection. 1 12 Resident essential: ESBL and AmpC are not interchangeable labels ESBL enzymes are most often encountered in E. coli , K. pneumoniae , and K. oxytoca and inactivate most penicillins, cephalosporins, and aztreonam. Carbapenems generally remain active. For organisms at moderate risk of clinically significant inducible AmpC, the 2026 IDSA guidance identifies E. cloacae complex, K. aerogenes , C. freundii , and H. alvei . Cefepime is generally effective when the MIC is in the susceptible or susceptible-dose-dependent range; ceftriaxone is not suggested for invasive infection with these organisms. 1 HECK-Yes is a memory aid: Hafnia alvei , Enterobacter cloacae complex, Citrobacter freundii , Klebsiella aerogenes , and Yersinia enterocolitica . Approach to a reported penicillin allergy Use the treating institution’s allergy assessment pathway for patient-specific decisions. Start with the history. Document the drug, timing, symptoms, treatment required, time since the reaction, and any beta-lactams tolerated afterward. Most reported penicillin allergies are not confirmed as current IgE-mediated allergy, but an incomplete history should be clarified rather than dismissed. 4 Classify the reaction before choosing another beta-lactam History Typical features Resident action Intolerance or nonallergic history Isolated nausea, diarrhea, headache, family history, or a label entered without a patient reaction. Document the history accurately. These findings alone do not establish immune-mediated allergy. Possible immediate IgE-mediated reaction Urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis beginning within minutes to several hours. Confirm the culprit drug and timing. Follow the local allergy pathway and review side-chain relationships before selecting therapy. Benign delayed eruption Morbilliform or maculopapular rash appearing after several days, without mucosal lesions, blistering, systemic illness, or organ injury. Clarify the phenotype and subsequent tolerance. Selected patients may qualify for supervised challenge under the local pathway. Severe delayed or organ-specific reaction SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, drug-induced liver injury, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or immune thrombocytopenia. Do not use PEN-FAST to clear the allergy or proceed to routine challenge. Avoid the culprit and obtain Allergy/Immunology or specialist guidance. PEN-FAST Scoring F: reaction within 5 years, or timing unknown: 2 points A or S: anaphylaxis or angioedema, or a severe cutaneous adverse reaction: 2 points T: treatment required, or treatment unknown: 1 point Interpretation 0: very low risk, less than 1% 1–2: low risk, about 5% 3: moderate risk, about 20% 4–5: high risk, about 50% Use PEN-FAST as a triage tool, not an order. A score below 3 had a negative predictive value of 96.3% in the original study. 13 The PEN-FAST calculator can help organize the history, but residents should not independently remove the allergy label or order a test dose or oral challenge. Suspected severe delayed reactions follow a separate pathway. Testing, challenge, and desensitization Skin testing Penicillin skin testing evaluates immediate IgE-mediated allergy. It may be followed by an oral amoxicillin challenge. It does not evaluate SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, interstitial nephritis, serum sickness, hemolytic anemia, or other serious non-IgE reactions. When to involve Allergy/Immunology Consult when the allergy is forcing clearly inferior therapy, when the patient is likely to need repeated antibiotics because of transplant, chemotherapy, or another immunocompromising condition, or when several antimicrobial allergy labels substantially limit treatment. Graded challenge A graded challenge assesses whether a low-risk patient tolerates the drug. It does not induce temporary tolerance. The eligibility and supervision for a challenge depend on the clinical setting and the evaluating team. Desensitization Desensitization induces temporary tolerance when the preferred drug is required and an appropriate alternative is not available. It requires a supervised protocol and uninterrupted dosing. It is not a routine approach to severe delayed reactions. Cross-reactivity Cross-reactivity is driven mainly by R1 side-chain similarity. For an unverified nonanaphylactic penicillin allergy without a severe delayed phenotype, the 2022 practice parameter supports routine cephalosporin administration without testing or added precautions. A structurally dissimilar cephalosporin such as cefazolin can also be given routinely after penicillin anaphylaxis under the practice parameter. Carbapenem cross-reactivity is very low, and the practice parameter supports carbapenem administration without testing or added precautions after penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, including anaphylaxis. Severe delayed reactions still require separate review. 4 Side-chain relationships worth remembering Index allergy Higher-concern related drug Clinical significance Amoxicillin Cefadroxil These share the same R1 side chain. A convincing immediate amoxicillin reaction deserves specific review before cefadroxil is used. Ampicillin Cephalexin and cefaclor These have identical or closely related amino R1 side chains. Do not treat an ampicillin allergy label as a class-wide cephalosporin ban, but do not ignore the phenotype when choosing one of these drugs. Ceftazidime Aztreonam These share an identical R1 side chain. A convincing immediate or severe ceftazidime reaction should prompt allergy-guided review before aztreonam. Cefazolin No commonly used beta-lactam shares its R1 side chain An isolated cefazolin allergy does not automatically predict a reaction to penicillins or other cephalosporins. Base the decision on the reaction phenotype. The bedside table above lists the relationships most likely to change a resident's immediate decision. For a complete matrix, see the public Northwestern Medicine cross-reactivity chart . 4 35 41
